title: Fewest hops: breadth-first search
summary: A queue visits everything 1 hop away, then 2, then 3, so the first time you reach a node is the shortest way.

say.never: Drop a stone in a pond. The ripple reaches everything 1 step away, then 2 steps, then 3. A **breadth-first search** spreads the same way. Instead of a stack it uses a **queue**, like a line at the cafeteria: `addLast` joins the back, `removeFirst` serves the front. Because the closest nodes are always served first, the first time you reach a node, you got there in the **fewest hops**.
say.bit: **Breadth-first search** uses a queue (first in, first out), so the first time it reaches a node is with the fewest hops.

say.never: The search finds the goal, but how did it get there? Leave a trail. Each time you find a new node, write down which node you came from, in a `Map`. That map also works as your visited set: if a node is already a key, you've seen it. At the goal, follow the trail backwards: the goal, where it came from, where *that* came from, all the way to the start. Add each one to the front of a list (`add(0, ...)`) and the list comes out in the right order.
say.bit: Keep a `Map` of node -> node you came from (it doubles as visited). At the goal, walk it back to the start, adding to the front.

steps.title: In your lesson: Leave a trail

say.never: `shortestPath` puts `from` on the queue and in the trail map. Each time you take a waypoint off the front, look at its neighbors. Any neighbor that isn't in the trail yet goes in the trail (came from here) and on the back of the queue. When the search is done, if `to` isn't in the trail, there's no path: return an empty list. Otherwise walk the trail back from `to` to `from`.
say.bit: Queue + trail map. New neighbor: record where it came from, `addLast` it. No `to` in the trail: empty list. Else walk back.
